metadata.title: Godot Shader Language
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How to read any shader, one type at a time
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Godot Shader Language. Learn how a shader file is built, what its types and vectors mean, and how to read any shader line by line, even one an AI wrote for you.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. When you first read shader code, it is natural to assume each line works on one number at a time. It does not. Many values in a shader are bundles of numbers, and one operator works on the whole bundle at once.

show.event: backspaces 'one number' and types 'a bundle of numbers'

props.text:
A shader line works on
one number at a time.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A pixel is one dot of the picture. A type is the kind of value something holds. A function is a named block of code you can call. An argument is a value you hand it.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
one dot of the picture on screen
the kind of value something holds: whole number, decimal, bundle
a named block of code you can call
a value you hand to a function when you call it

beats.act: I · The Shape of a File
beats.narration_text: A shader file has three zones, read from the top down. The header says what kind of shader this is. The globals are values declared outside every function. The functions are where the work happens.

shot.visual_intent: The same 14-line file alone on the stage (layout 'code', line numbers on). Three bands light in turn with a one-word chip beside each: line 1 'header', lines 3 to 4 'globals', lines 6 to 14 'functions'.
shot.motion_claim: A highlight band slides down the file and stops on each zone as the voice names it.

lecture.why: A Manim card at the 32-point type floor holds about 8 lines of code (measured: Menlo at 32 is 0.25 unit per character, 0.6 per line); ShaderLab's code layout shows all 14 real lines.

beats.act: I · The Shape of a File
beats.narration_text: The header starts with shader type, and it must be the first line. Canvas item means two-D drawing and interface. Spatial means three-D. An optional second line, render mode, picks options, such as how a pixel blends with the background.

shot.visual_intent: `shader_type canvas_item;` in monospace (size 40) upper center. Under it a row of tiles: `canvas_item` captioned '2D + interface' and `spatial` captioned '3D' (both outlined), and three small tiles `particles`, `sky`, `fog` under a bracket labelled 'more'. A terracotta ring settles on canvas_item, in the line and on its tile. Serif 32 caption: 'shader type: the first line; says what the shader is for'. Last, a dimmer second line `render_mode blend_add;` slides in below with a tag 'optional' and a drawn pair of overlapping outlined squares whose overlap is tinted lighter, labelled 'blend'.

show.event: render_mode line slides in, tagged optional

shot.motion_claim: The first line types in and the tiles line up under it; a ring picks canvas item; then an optional second line slides in below.

lecture.why: The first line is the picture; tiles under the real line show what the line chooses, which a table would only list.

beats.act: I · The Shape of a File
beats.narration_text: Globals sit outside every function. A uniform is a value your game sets from outside. A const never changes. A varying hands a value from a shape's corners to its pixels. Declare each one above the code that uses it.

shot.visual_intent: A band labelled 'globals' with three rows stacked, each a declaration copied from lab-shaders/04-globals.gdshader in monospace with a serif 32 caption beneath in the GLOSSARY wording: `uniform float level = 0.8;` / 'a value your game sets from outside; every pixel sees the same one'; `const vec3 TEAL = vec3(0.37, 0.64, 0.57);` / 'a named value that never changes'; `varying vec2 corner_uv;` / 'a value set at each corner, blended across the shape for fragment() to read'. Below the band a thin bar labelled 'functions' and a drawn downward arrow from the band into it, labelled 'readable below'. Captions may wrap to two lines.
shot.motion_claim: The three declarations land one by one as they are named; a downward arrow then runs from them into the functions bar.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: Three declarations with their one-line meanings, and the direction they are visible in, are a structure drawn on cue; a table cannot show the arrow.

beats.act: I · The Shape of a File
beats.narration_text: Then come the functions. Godot calls three of them for you. Vertex places the corners, fragment sets the color of each pixel, and light handles each light that touches a pixel. This film uses fragment. Any other function is one you write yourself.

shot.visual_intent: A three-row table in the GLOSSARY wording, one row ringed as each function is named: vertex(), fragment(), light().

props.title: The functions Godot calls
rows: once for each pixel the shape covers
once per pixel, for each light that touches it

shot.motion_claim: The ring steps down the rows with the voice; fragment() stays ringed longest.

lecture.why: Three terms are defined here for the first time, and a table of kinds is exactly what the evidence-table component is for.

beats.act: I · The Shape of a File
beats.narration_text: Inside a function, every statement ends with a semicolon, and braces group statements into a block. Forget one semicolon and Godot refuses the whole shader. Here it points at the next line, where it noticed.

shot.visual_intent: A terminal window titled 'Godot 4.7.2 · shader compile error · printed by the engine' holding the engine's own log of lab-shaders/40-err-semicolon.gdshader, word for word: the source lines around the error with the offending line marked, then the error message. A terracotta ring lands on the marked line (the line AFTER the one missing its semicolon) late in the beat.

beats.act: I · The Shape of a File
beats.narration_text: Spacing and line breaks are for people. Here is one shader that draws a soft gradient, written three ways: neat, squeezed onto one line, and spread over many. Godot draws the same picture for all three.

The characters slide and the line breaks collapse and reopen as one spelling becomes the next. Bottom region, never changing: ONE framed real Godot render (lab_window of png/02-spacing-neat.png, a pastel gradient) captioned 'Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+', with a drawn equals sign (two short bars) between code and picture, labelled 'same picture'. beats.act: I · The Shape of a File
beats.narration_text: Comments are notes for people. Two slashes comment out the rest of a line. Slash star starts a block comment, and star slash ends it. Godot skips both, so a commented-out line does nothing.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the nine-line card of lab-shaders/03-comment-on.gdshader with a block comment above the function and a trailing `// soften` comment: both comment spans are grayed from the first frame. Right: a framed real render (lab_window of png/03-comment-on.png, the pastel gradient). Then `//` is typed at the start of the line `c = 0.4 + 0.6 * c;` (the line grays out, as in lab-shaders/03-comment-off.gdshader) and the render cross-fades to the real png/03-comment-off.png (the same colors, much more saturated, dark top-left corner). Captions: 'line comment', 'block comment'.

beats.act: I · The Shape of a File
beats.narration_text: Godot's language is close to G L S L, the shading language of OpenGL, but not identical. Names must match exactly, capitals included: a capital L makes level a different name. The other language's G L frag color is unknown here. Godot calls it color.

shot.visual_intent: Two panels. Left: two name tags in monospace, `level` with a drawn check and `Level` with a drawn cross, a drawn capital-L highlight on the difference. Right: `gl_FragColor` with a drawn cross, a drawn arrow to `COLOR` with a drawn check, captioned 'Godot's name for the output'. Top caption in serif 32: 'GLSL: the OpenGL Shading Language; Godot's is close to GLSL ES 3.0'. No engine messages on screen (the narration says unknown identifier).

show.event: cross on Level, capital L highlighted
gl_FragColor crossed; arrow to COLOR; check

shot.motion_claim: A cross lands on the wrong-case name and on the other language's name; the check lands on Godot's.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: Two kinds of wrong name (wrong case, other language) are a contrast of name tags with marks; the logs for both were run and are in the evidence.

beats.narration_text: Every value has a type. A float is a decimal number, an int is a whole number, and a bool is true or false. A texture has a type too, called sampler two D. You declare a variable with its type first, then its name.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Types and Vectors' (serif 40) top-left. Four outlined tiles in a row, each a type with a sample value in monospace: `float` / 0.5, `int` / 3, `bool` / true, `sampler2D` / a small drawn picture icon (a framed square with a hill shape). Under each tile a plain label: 'a decimal number', 'a whole number', 'true or false', 'the type of a texture a shader reads'. A one-line serif 32 caption under the row, in the GLOSSARY wording: 'texture: an image a shader can read by address'. Below, the declaration `float level = 0.5;` (a line of lab-shaders/32-declaration.gdshader) with three drawn brackets under it labelled 'type', 'name', 'value'.

show.event: act title; float, int, bool tiles pop in

beats.narration_text: Godot is strict about this. A two with no decimal point is an int, and Godot will not quietly turn it into a float. Put it in a float, or add it to one, and the shader will not compile. Write two point zero.

shot.visual_intent: A terminal window holding two short excerpts of the engine's own log, word for word and separated by a blank line: the marked line `float a = 2;` with 'Invalid assignment of 'int' to 'float'.' and the marked line `float a = 1 + 1.0;` with 'Invalid arguments to operator '+': 'int, float'.' A ring lands on each message.

beats.narration_text: Shaders are full of vectors, bundles of two to four numbers: vec two, vec three, vec four. A color is a vec four: red, green, blue and alpha, how solid it is. Reading a texture gives back a vec four too.

shot.visual_intent: Rows of outlined cells (the bundle cast), stacked: `vec2` two cells, `vec3` three cells, `vec4` four cells labelled r g b a, the vec4 cells holding 0.37, 0.64, 0.57, 1.0 with a plain teal swatch to its right labelled 'a color'. Far left of the vec4 row, a framed small drawn texture (gradient square) with a drawn arrow into the row, labelled 'texture lookup'. Serif 32 caption: 'vector: a bundle of two to four numbers'. Under the last cell, in the GLOSSARY wording, 'alpha: how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid'.

show.event: vec4 row with r g b a and swatch

beats.narration_text: You build a vector by naming its type. Give vec three one number and it fills all three parts. Give vec four a vec three and a number and it joins them. The pieces must add up to the size, or Godot refuses.

shot.visual_intent: Three mini-diagrams stacked, using the bundle cells. (1) `vec3(0.5)`: one cell [0.5] sprouts two copies to make [0.5][0.5][0.5]. (2) `vec4(c, 1.0)`: a three-cell bundle c and a one-cell [1.0] slide together into a four-cell bundle, a drawn counter 3 + 1 = 4. (3) `vec3(0.1, 0.2)`: two cells and a dashed empty cell with a drawn cross, counter 2 of 3, labelled 'too few'.

show.event: three plus one join into four
two cells and a gap: crossed

shot.motion_claim: Cells copy, slide together and join into a bundle of the right size; the short one is refused.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: Constructing a vector is cells joining; the sizes adding up is a counter you can watch.

beats.narration_text: Arithmetic works on every part at once. Multiply a vec three by two point zero and all three numbers double. Multiply two vectors and each part meets its partner. That is why shader code is so short.

shot.visual_intent: Top: a three-cell bundle (0.2, 0.3, 0.4), a drawn times sign, a single cell 2.0; three parallel drawn arrows leave the 2.0 for each cell at the same instant; the result bundle (0.4, 0.6, 0.8) appears. Bottom: the same bundle times a second bundle (2.0, 1.0, 0.5); three short drawn arrows pair cell to cell, top to bottom; the result (0.4, 0.3, 0.2). Labels in monospace: `* 2.0`, `* vec3(2.0, 1.0, 0.5)`.

show.event: bundle times bundle, cell to cell

shot.motion_claim: Three arrows fire at the same instant and all three numbers change together; then each part meets its partner.

lecture.why: 'Every part at once' is simultaneous motion; three arrows leaving one cell in the same frame is the claim.

beats.narration_text: Here it is in use. U V is the address of each pixel, a vec two. Join it with one half to make a vec three, scale by zero point six, add zero point four. Red grows to the right, green grows downward.

shot.visual_intent: Code panel at left with the five-line shader; at right a framed real render: a pastel gradient, red growing to the right and green growing downward, blue constant. Short readouts 'more red' near the top-right corner and 'more green' near the bottom-left corner. Caption under the render: 'UV: a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down'.

beats.narration_text: You can reach into a vector by name. Dot R G B takes red, green and blue from a vec four. Dot X Y takes the first two parts. Picking or reordering parts like this is called swizzling.

shot.visual_intent: A four-cell vec4 row with THREE label rows: x y z w above the cells, r g b a below them, and a fainter s t p q under those (the third set, for texture coordinates). A drawn bracket over the first three cells labelled `.rgb` lifts them out into a three-cell vec3 row; then a bracket over the first two labelled `.xy` lifts them into a two-cell vec2 row. Serif 32 caption: 'swizzle: picking or reordering a vector's parts'.

beats.narration_text: Order is yours to choose. Dot B G R reverses the order, and the gradient's colors turn over. R G B A, X Y Z W and S T P Q name the same parts, but never mix sets in one swizzle. Godot refuses.

beats.narration_text: To read any line, say the type of each piece, from the inside out. U V is a vec two. Joined with one half, a vec three. Times a float, still a vec three. Plus a float, still a vec three.

beats.narration_text: Now your own functions. The first line of a function is its signature. It has three parts: the type it hands back, its name, and its arguments, each with a type.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Your Own Functions' (serif 40) top-left. The line `vec3 soften(vec3 c) {` in monospace (size 40) centered, with the body line `return 0.4 + 0.6 * c;` and a closing brace beneath it. Three drawn brackets under the first line land in order, each with a plain label: under `vec3` 'hands back', under `soften` 'name', under `(vec3 c)` 'arguments, each with a type'. Serif 32 caption: 'signature: the first line of a function'.
shot.motion_claim: Three brackets close in turn round the type, the name and the argument list.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: A signature is three parts of one line; brackets that close on each part in order are the clearest way to separate them.

beats.narration_text: Calling the function hands values into the arguments, in order. The body runs. Then return hands one value back, and it must have the type the signature promised. Break that promise and Godot says so.

shot.visual_intent: At left the call `soften(vec3(UV, 0.5))`; a small three-cell token travels along a drawn path into the argument slot `c` of a rounded box that holds `return 0.4 + 0.6 * c;`; the box pulses; a new three-cell token leaves the box and returns to the call, tagged 'vec3, as promised'. Then a four-cell token leaves the box instead and bounces off a drawn bar with a cross, with the engine's message in two short lines under it: `Expected return with an expression` / `of type 'vec3'.`
shot.motion_claim: A bundle goes into the function and a bundle comes back out; a bundle of the wrong size bounces.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: In and out is a flow; a token entering and leaving the box makes 'hands values in, hands one value back' literal.

beats.narration_text: Godot reads from the top down. A function must be defined above the one that calls it. Call it first and the message says no matching function found. It does not say the order is wrong.

beats.narration_text: A function you write cannot see most built-ins. A built-in is a value the engine hands to a function. U V and color are handed to fragment, not to your function. Use U V inside yours and Godot says unknown identifier.

shot.visual_intent: Two rounded boxes: right, `fragment()` containing three outlined chips `UV`, `COLOR`, `TEXTURE`; left, a box `soften()` of your own. A thick gray vertical wall stands between them. The UV chip leaves fragment, crosses toward the function, hits the wall and bounces back; a small drawn bubble near the bounce reads 'unknown identifier'. Serif 32 caption: 'built-in: a value the engine hands to a function, or collects from it'.

beats.narration_text: Arguments come in three modes. In, the default, hands over a copy, so changes stay inside the function. In out hands over the original, so the caller's variable changes. Out is for writing a result back.

shot.visual_intent: Top strip: three chips with one-to-three-word captions, `in` 'a copy', `inout` 'the original', `out` 'writes back'; the active chip is ringed. Middle: the caller's variable box `a = 0.25`. Bottom: the function signature card, which changes with the active mode. IN (`float bump(float x)`): a ghost copy of 0.25 goes into the function, becomes 0.75 and returns to `b`; the box a still reads 0.25. INOUT (`void bump(inout float x)`): a double-headed drawn arrow ties the function to the box a itself, which changes to 0.75. OUT (`void make(out vec3 c)`): the function writes (0.1, 0.5, 0.9) into an empty three-cell box c in the caller.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A shader file has a header, globals and functions. Every value has a type, and Godot will not quietly convert between int and float. Many values are vectors, and arithmetic works on every part at once. A function has a signature, and per-pixel built-ins must be passed in. Choices need a bool, and floats are compared against a range. To read a line, say the type of each piece.
